name: Tokyo
description: Marunouchi to Tokyo Tower from open data, lit by the real sun. Every building height is a PLATEAU survey value, and every shadow is computed.

protection.title: No sun-access rule: a lunch-hour test
protection.summary: Tokyo has no rule that protects sun on parks and plazas. The windows here are a thought experiment for this project: what would a new tower cost the lunch hour?
protection.source_note: Windows are our own choice (noon to 13:00, all year), not law. Tokyo's shadow rule, 日影規制 (Building Standards Act, art. 56-2), limits hours of shadow on neighbouring land in designated residential-type zones; it does not cover public places and does not apply in commercial districts such as Marunouchi. Check the ward's zoning before relying on this.
protection.reading_note: Tokyo keeps standard time all year (no daylight saving), so the clock and the sun agree all year. Baseline: the test compares against today's PLATEAU model, which is surveyed to 2020-ish, so towers built since are missing from 76% of the footprint area's heights unless Overture or OSM has them.
protection.tip: Tip: try the block south-west of Hibiya Park, or between the Marunouchi towers and the Palace.

tour.title: Marunouchi to Tokyo Tower, from open data
tour.text: {buildings} buildings. {share:plateau}% of the footprint area stands at a height that Project PLATEAU surveyed, on GSI 5 m laser-scanned bare earth under GSI aerial photos.

tour.title: Tokyo Station and the air above it
tour.text: Tokyo Station's red-brick Marunouchi building was restored in 2012. The unused floor area above it was sold to the towers around it, so the old station stays low while Marunouchi grows tall. Compare it with JP Tower, behind it, at 200 m.

tour.title: Hibiya Park at lunch
tour.text: On the winter solstice, {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|12:00}% of Hibiya Park is in direct sun at noon, and {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|13:00}% at 13:00. On 21 June at noon it is {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|6-21|12:00}%. No rule protects either.

tour.title: Where the heights come from
tour.text: Blue: surveyed height (PLATEAU or OpenStreetMap). Orange: floor count. Green: estimated. In the model, PLATEAU's roof surveys give every tower in Marunouchi, Shiodome and Toranomon its real massing, podium and all.

tour.title: Tokyo Tower at sunset
tour.text: 333 m, painted in bands of International Orange and white because aircraft must see it. The lattice is built from published dimensions, anchored at the tower's published coordinates.

tour.title: After dark
tour.text: Windows light from the same facade grid that shades them by day. Drag to explore, or open Sun access to test a tower of your own.

sources.landmarks: Tokyo Tower: parametric from published dimensions (333 m; decks at 150 m and 250 m; 80 m base), anchored at its published coordinates

game.title: Tokyo on Foot
game.ferry_note: Piers are from OpenStreetMap via Overture. Routes are generated through open water; the stops follow the real water-bus piers, but the timetable is not real, and the vessel names are those of Tokyo Cruise boats. Boats run at 1.5 times their real speed and wait 20 s at each pier. At a pier you can skip the wait.

npcs.name: Haruka 遥
idle: 指差呼称 (shisa kanko): we point at every signal and say it aloud, even when no train is coming. Fewer mistakes, they say, by a lot.
Trains here run to the second. If one is 20 seconds late, we apologise. {time} now.

npcs.name: Kenji 健二
idle: Until 1963 Tokyo capped buildings at 31 m, a hundred shaku. Then floor-area ratios replaced the cap.
I eat at my desk or in Hibiya Park, if the sun's out. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Daichi 大地
npcs.role: Palace runner 皇居ランナー
idle: Five kilometres round the Palace, always counter-clockwise. 反時計回り. Nobody told me; everybody does it.
Evening is busiest. By 18:00 you queue at the lockers.

npcs.name: Sachiko 幸子
idle: Hibiya Park opened in 1903, Japan's first Western-style park. My grandmother walked in it in a kimono.

npcs.name: Yui 結衣
idle: Ginza at lunch: the main street closes to cars on weekend afternoons. 歩行者天国, the pedestrian paradise.
Lunch is 12:00 to 13:00. Everyone in Marunouchi comes out at once.

npcs.name: Ishikawa-san 石川
idle: いらっしゃいませ! Under the tracks since 1985. The trains overhead? That's the seasoning.
Brick arches from 1910, and every arch is somebody's bar.

npcs.name: Captain Aoki 青木船長
idle: Edo's shogun hunted ducks at Hamarikyu. Now the ducks watch Shiodome's towers.
The Sumida River ends here, and the bay begins. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Hayashi 林
idle: The cabin's warm. Keep clear of the Tokyo Tower lattice: 333 m of steel, and it does not move.

npcs.name: Ren 蓮
idle: Tokyo Tower opened in 1958, at 333 m, 13 m taller than the Eiffel Tower. That was the point.
The orange-and-white paint is for aircraft. It repaints every five years.

npcs.name: Mei 芽依
idle: Navy blazer, a ribbon, and a long walk to school. I love the autumn light on the moat.
My cram school is in Otemachi. It's {time}. {sun_line}

quests.title: Welcome to Tokyo Station
talk: ようこそ。Welcome. You're the new surveyor? This city is rebuilt from open data: {buildings} buildings, laser-scanned terrain, the real sun.
This is the Marunouchi side: red brick, built 1914, restored 2012. Behind it, the glass towers. Kenji works in one of them, on Marunouchi Naka-dori.
WASD or the arrow keys to walk, Shift to run, drag to look around. E to talk.

quests.title: The air above the station
talk: Look at the station: a few storeys of brick. Look at the towers: 200 m of glass. Why does Marunouchi look like that?
Because the station owner sold its unused floor area, its 空中権 (air rights), to the towers nearby. The brick stays low and the money restored it.

Here every building carries the source of its height. {share:plateau}% of the footprint area comes from PLATEAU's roof surveys. Aim at a building and press Q to use the survey lens. Find a surveyed one, a floor-count one and an estimate.

steps.text: Survey lens (Q): a PLATEAU, a floor-count and an estimated height
Find Daichi on the Palace plaza

quests.title: Round the Palace
talk: Cooling down. This gravel plaza is the Kokyo Gaien; the moat is Edo Castle's. Edo became Tokyo in 1868.
Yui says lunch is the best hour in Hibiya Park, if the sun's out. Winter, though. In December the sun sits low, and the towers matter. Ask Sachiko.

quests.title: A bench in the sun
talk: Winter lunch in Hibiya Park: that's my favourite hour. On 22 December at noon, {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|12-22|12:00}% of the park is in direct sun. On 21 June it's {sun:Hibiya Park 日比谷公園|6-21|12:00}%.
No rule protects it, you know. A new tower could take it away. Find a sunny spot for me at lunchtime on the winter solstice. Watch the sun meter under the map. It ray-casts from where you stand.

steps.text: Stand in direct sun in Hibiya Park, 12:00 to 13:00 on 22 December

quests.title: Lunch in Ginza
talk: Finally, someone who counts shadows! Ginza's main street keeps its wall at 56 m under the Ginza Rules (銀座ルール). Check it with Q.
Skip the department store, though. Ishikawa-san grills under the tracks at Yurakucho, and his yakitori is the real lunch.

steps.text: Find Ishikawa-san under the Yurakucho tracks

quests.title: Water bus
talk: いらっしゃい! Eat. Tokyo is a city of water: the Palace moat, the canals, and the bay out there. Most people forget.
Walk down to Hamarikyu, the shogun's garden. The water bus leaves from the pier. Ride it to Hinode Pier, and tell Captain Aoki I sent you.

steps.text: Take the water bus from Hamarikyu to Hinode Pier
Find Captain Aoki at Hinode Pier

quests.title: Tokyo Tower from the air
talk: From the water the city is a wall. Go up. Hayashi's helicopter is on the pad in Hibiya Park.

Fly south-west to Tokyo Tower and land in Shiba Park below it. Space to climb, C to descend, W and S for forward and back, A and D to turn. V is the bird's-eye view. E gets you out once you've landed.

steps.text: Meet Hayashi at the Hibiya Park helipad
Land in Shiba Park, below Tokyo Tower
Find Ren at the foot of Tokyo Tower

quests.title: 333 metres
talk: You flew in? Then you've seen it: {landmark:tokyo_tower.height} m, and the main deck at {landmark:tokyo_tower.main_deck} m. The model builds the lattice from those figures, not from a scan.
Not everything is a scan, anyway. {share:plateau}% of the buildings you passed were surveyed by PLATEAU; the rest are estimates from their neighbours.
Report back to Haruka at the station. The survey is nearly done.

steps.text: Report back to Haruka at Tokyo Station

quests.title: Survey complete
talk: お疲れ様でした。That's the full survey: the station, the air above it, the Palace, the sun, the water and the tower.
Now you know where the numbers come from. The city is yours. Change the time of day, take the water bus, or fly anywhere.
